analysis.one_liner: Bans new federal leases for coal, oil, and gas on public lands and offshore waters.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate on December 18, 2024 with three cosponsors, sent to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and never taken up before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop the Interior Department from issuing or renewing leases for coal, oil, natural gas, tar sands, and oil shale on federal land, and would bar all new offshore drilling leases in the Arctic, Atlantic, Pacific, and Gulf of Mexico. It would also cancel existing federal leases in the Beaufort Sea, Cook Inlet, and Chukchi Sea within 60 days. Its stated goal is to keep federal fossil fuels underground to limit global warming, with narrow exceptions for national security threats and contract disputes. The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be the public at large through reduced greenhouse gas emissions from federal lands and waters, which the bill's findings say account for a significant share of the emissions budget needed to stay under 2 degrees Celsius of warming [S2]. Communities exposed to drilling and mining pollution, coastal and Arctic communities, and people who bear climate-related costs like wildfire, flood, and heat damage would gain. Renewable energy industries would gain market ground as fossil fuel leasing on federal land ends.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone exposed to climate and drilling impacts

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Interior Department from issuing, renewing, reinstating, or extending any lease for oil, gas, or other fossil fuels anywhere on the outer Continental Shelf, including the Arctic, Atlantic, Pacific, and the Gulf of Mexico [S2].
Prohibits new onshore federal leases for coal, oil, tar sands, oil shale, and gas, and blocks renewing nonproducing leases [S2].
Requires cancellation, within 60 days of enactment, of existing federal leases in the Beaufort Sea, Cook Inlet, and Chukchi Sea [S2].
Includes exceptions only for leases needed to address an imminent national security threat, or where enforcing the ban would amount to a material breach of a pre-existing lease contract [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal companies that lease federal land and waters would lose access to new federal supplies and, in the Arctic, existing leases. Federal, state, tribal, and local governments would lose royalty revenue that funds public services. Energy-producing regions, including coal towns and Gulf Coast and Alaska communities built around extraction, would face job and revenue losses, and consumers could face somewhat higher energy prices if federal supply cuts tighten markets.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel companies and energy-producing regions

drawbacks.text: Ending federal leasing would cut off royalty payments shared with states, tribes, and the Treasury, and would reduce revenue and jobs in coal and oil-producing regions that depend on federal leases [S2].

Restricting supply could raise energy prices for consumers, particularly if domestic production falls faster than demand, and the bill addresses demand or transition support for displaced workers and communities not at all [S2].
Cancelling existing Arctic leases within 60 days could invite costly legal challenges over contract and property rights, which is partly why the bill includes a breach-of-contract exception [S2].
The bill is unilateral: it restricts American federal supply but does not by itself reduce global demand for fossil fuels, so opponents argue emissions and prices shift rather than fall.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is long-term and shared broadly: keeping the majority of federal fossil fuel reserves unleased reduces the emissions driving climate change, at real but localized cost to extractive industries and the communities and governments that depend on royalty revenue. Its serious design gap is that it offers no transition plan — no worker support, no revenue replacement, no demand-side policy — which is a fair criticism even for supporters. As written, it is an all-or-nothing prohibition with narrow exceptions, and it had no realistic path to passage in this Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 18, 2024, read twice, and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where it sat with no hearing or vote until the Congress ended two weeks later.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on December 18, 2024, joined by Senators Sanders, Warren, and Markey as original cosponsors [S2].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources on the day of introduction [S1].
It had three cosponsors total — one Independent and two Democrats — and no action beyond referral before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal companies that hold or seek federal leases kept the status quo: no hearings, no vote, no restrictions, and the Congress expired with the bill dead. Governments and communities that rely on federal royalty revenue were also spared disruption, while the emissions reductions the bill targeted did not happen.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel companies holding federal leases

sides.party_line_note: All support came from Democrats and one Independent, with no Republican cosponsor and no recorded votes; the bill died in committee without any floor action.

industries.industry: Coal mining companies with federal leases
industries.note: The bill bars all new federal coal leases and renewals of nonproducing leases, cutting off future access to public-land coal. Its profits come from extracting fuel the bill's findings identify as a primary driver of warming.

New offshore leasing would be banned everywhere on the outer Continental Shelf and existing Arctic leases cancelled, eliminating future federal acreage. Offshore drilling imposes spill and climate risks on coastal communities.

industries.industry: Onshore oil, gas, tar sands, and oil shale operators on federal land
industries.note: No new federal leases, lease sales, or renewals of nonproducing leases would be allowed. Operators would be limited to already-producing leases until they expire.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and clean technology industries
industries.note: With federal fossil fuel leasing shut off, market and policy momentum shifts toward clean energy buildout, which the bill names as a policy goal. Communities near clean energy projects share in the benefit, though the bill provides no direct subsidies.
